Then "every time" looks perfect but only measures one try. Turn caching off, keep normal settings, or vary how each request is worded.

**2. The grader is shaky too.** If another LLM judges pass or fail, the judge can change its mind between tries. Its wobble gets counted as the agent failing. Spot-check the judge's verdicts by hand, or use plain checks where you can, like "was the refund recorded?"

**3. Very few tasks or tries.** With 10 tasks and 3 tries, one unlucky try can flip a whole task. Two agent versions may then look different when they are not. Add more tasks before trusting small gaps. Also rerun the whole test and see how much the two shares move.

learn:term.a:
**pass@k** means "the task passed **at least once** in k tries." The k is just the number of tries. With 3 tries, it's written pass@3.

**Everyday comparison:** picture a contest where you get three shots and only your best one counts. Sink one out of three and you're through. The misses don't matter.

That fits when a person looks at all the attempts and keeps the best one. It's a forgiving score.

**In the lesson's example:**
- `refund` passed all three tries. It counts.
- `address` passed on tries 1 and 3 but failed try 2. It still counts, because one pass is enough.
- `cancel` failed every try. It doesn't count.

So 2 of 3 tasks pass, and pass@3 is 2 of 3.

Notice that `address` scores just as well as `refund` here. That's what pass@k hides. It can't tell a lucky agent from a reliable one.

Its stricter partner, pass^k ("pass hat k"), only counts tasks that pass every time. Each real user gets just one try, so the stricter count is closer to what users actually experience.

check:0:0.q: Why not “To keep each answer short and to the point”?
check:0:0.a:
It's a reasonable guess, because both ideas involve "limits." But they limit different things.

A step limit doesn't touch the length of any answer. It counts **rounds of the loop**. One round is the model picking a tool, then your code running it. With `recursion_limit` set to 25, LangGraph stops after about 12 rounds, no matter how long or short each message is.

If you want shorter answers, you use other tools. You can ask for brevity in the prompt (the instructions you send the model). Or you can cap the number of tokens, which are the small chunks of text the model reads and writes.

What the option misses is the real danger. A confused model might call the same tool again and again and never give a final answer. Every round is another paid model call. LangGraph's built-in limit is about 10,000 steps, so a stuck agent could spend a lot before anything stops it.

"A confused model can loop forever, spending money" is the better answer because it names the actual risk: a loop that never ends, and the bill that keeps growing.

check:0:1.q: Why not “The model API refuses runs that have no limit”?
check:0:1.a:
It's a tempting answer, because it sounds like someone else is keeping you safe. But that isn't how the loop works.

**What it gets right:** limits do matter, and some tools do have them. LangGraph, for example, has a built-in recursion limit (its name for a step limit).

**What it misses:** the model API is the online service that sends back one model reply each time you ask. It only sees one request at a time. It has no idea those requests are part of a loop. The loop lives in *your* code. So nothing on the model's side will refuse a run because it has no limit.

Even LangGraph's built-in limit won't save you. It's about 10,000 steps. A stuck agent can spend a lot of money before it hits that. That's why you set your own small limit, like `recursion_limit: 25`.

**Why the other option is right:** "A confused model can loop forever, spending money" names the real danger: the model can keep picking tools and never give a final answer, and every step costs you.

judge.notes: Passes. The claim that the model API never refuses unlimited runs goes beyond the lesson, but it doesn't contradict it.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Stop the whole run with a crash”?
check:1:0.a:
Crashing does get one thing right. It stops the agent from doing something wrong, and it makes the problem loud, so you notice it.

But it throws away too much. A **crash** means your program stops with an error and the whole run ends. Every step the agent already finished is lost. The user gets no answer at all.

And the mistake here is small. The model asked for a tool called `"weather"` that doesn't exist. Models make slips like this often. They guess a tool name or mix one up. That doesn't mean the whole task is hopeless.

A crash also gives the model no chance to learn what went wrong. It never sees the problem, so it can't fix it.

You might worry the model keeps asking for `"weather"` forever. Your small step limit covers that. The loop still ends.

So the right answer is "Send back an error the model can read." It's better because the model sees a message like "no tool named `weather`," can pick a real tool or answer another way, and the run keeps going.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Skip it quietly and ask the model again”?
check:1:2.a:
"Skip it quietly and ask the model again" gets one thing right. It doesn't crash. The loop keeps running, and that part is good.

The problem is the word "quietly." The model only knows what is in its **history**, the list of messages it reads each turn. If you skip the bad tool call and add nothing, the history looks exactly as it did before. So the model has no reason to change its mind. It will most likely ask for `"weather"` again, and again.

Each of those repeats uses up a step and costs money. Your step limit will stop it eventually. But you will have paid for every wasted round and got no answer. Skipping quietly also leaves no record of what went wrong, so the problem is harder to spot later.

**"Send back an error the model can read" is better.** A short note like "Unknown tool: weather" goes into the history, so the model learns that tool doesn't exist and can pick a real one or give a final answer.

check:2:0.q: Why not “A tool sends back an error”?
check:2:0.a:
It's a fair guess. Errors do happen in agents, and noticing them matters. But in a safe agent, an error doesn't stop the loop.

The lesson's second rule is to turn tool errors into messages the model can read, instead of crashes. A "crash" means the program halts with an error. So when a tool fails, your code writes the error into the history (the running list of messages the model sees). Then the loop goes around again. The model reads the error and can try another tool or fix its request.

That's the point of the rule. One bad tool call shouldn't end the whole job. The agent gets a chance to recover.

So a tool error is just another result fed back to the model. It isn't an exit.

There are two real ways out. One is the hard step limit, which is a safety stop for a stuck agent. This agent isn't stuck, so that doesn't apply here.

"The model gives a final answer" is better because it's the one normal, built-in exit: the model decides it's done and the loop returns its text.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Every tool has been used once”?
check:2:2.a:
It's a natural guess. In this example, the agent has used both tools it needed, so the job does feel done. That part of the thinking is fair.

But the loop never checks which tools have been used. Nothing in it keeps a tally. Look at the lesson's loop shape: each round, it asks the model for an action. Then it either returns, if `action.final` is true, or runs the tool and goes around again.

Tool use is also a poor signal of being done:

- An agent might call the same tool twice, say to look up two orders.
- It might never touch some tools at all, because the question didn't need them.

So "every tool used once" could stop too early or never happen.

The only other way out is the step limit. That's a safety net for stuck agents, and this agent isn't stuck.

"The model gives a final answer" is better because that is the one exit the loop checks on every round, and the model decides it when it has enough to reply.

judge.notes: Minor: calling the final answer 'the one exit' sits a bit awkwardly next to the step limit it also names, but nothing contradicts the lesson.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Always put a limit on agent loops” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
An agent loop has no natural end. It stops only when the model decides it is done. Sometimes it never decides.

A common way this happens: the model calls a **tool** (a function your code runs for it), gets a result it doesn't like, and calls the same tool again. And again. Each round is a new model call, and each call costs money.

A small example. You ask an agent, "What's the weather in Paris?" The weather tool returns an error because the city name is misspelled. The model tries the exact same call and gets the same error. Without your own limit, this keeps repeating. LangGraph's built-in limit is about 10,000 steps, so you could pay for thousands of useless calls first. Meanwhile, the user just sees a loading spinner.

With a small limit, say `recursion_limit` set to 25, the loop stops after about 12 rounds. LangGraph then raises a `GraphRecursionError`, an error that means "hit the step limit."

Pair the limit with a clear message, like "Stopped: too many steps." That tells you and the user what happened, instead of a silent hang or a confusing crash.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “A loop with a hard stop” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "An agent is a loop. The model picks a tool, my code runs it, the result goes back to the model, and it repeats until the model gives a final answer. If the model gets stuck, that loop can keep going, and every model call costs money."

*The idea:* "So I always set my own small step limit. In LangGraph that's `recursion_limit` in the config. I don't trust the default, which is about 10,000 steps. I also turn tool errors into messages the model can read, so one bad tool call doesn't crash the whole run."

*The trade-off:* "A limit that's too low can cut off a hard task that was nearly done. So I size it to the task, and I handle the stop cleanly."

**Likely follow-up:** "How do you pick the number, and what happens at the limit?"

*Hint:* Explain the counting. One model call plus its tool calls is 2 steps, because tools that run together count as one. So a limit of 25 allows about 12 rounds. At the limit, LangGraph raises `GraphRecursionError` (an error that means "too many steps"). A strong answer says you catch it, log it, and give the user a clear message.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Bills or token counts jump.** One user question triggers dozens or hundreds of model calls. A token is a small chunk of text the model reads or writes, and you pay per token.
- **The same tool repeats in the logs.** The trace (the step-by-step record of a run) shows the model calling one tool with the same input again and again. It is stuck.
- **Very long runs that end in `GraphRecursionError`.** If this error only appears after thousands of steps, nobody set a small limit. LangGraph's default of about 10,000 is doing the stopping, far too late.
- **Whole runs crash on one bad tool call.** A wrong tool name or a timeout gives a Python error and the run dies. The model never sees the problem, so it never gets a chance to fix it.
- **Fine in testing, failing in real use.** Test tools always work, so errors and loops never show up until real users arrive.

**Quickest check**

First, look at the `graph.invoke` call. Confirm its `config` sets a small `recursion_limit`, such as `25`. Then run one test where the model asks for a tool that doesn't exist. A healthy agent reads the error and carries on. A fragile one crashes.

judge.notes: No significant problems. It runs about 205 words, right at the length limit, and the claim that test tools always work goes slightly beyond the lesson.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Long tasks that really need many steps.** A research agent might honestly need 40 tool calls. A limit of 25 would cut it off mid-work with `GraphRecursionError`. Set the limit per kind of task. Also cap money or time spent. Save progress as you go (LangGraph calls this a **checkpoint**) so a stopped run can resume.

**2. Tools that change things in the real world.** Sending an email or charging a card is risky. If the tool fails and the model reads the error, it may just try again. That can mean two emails or two charges. Make such tools safe to repeat (**idempotent**: running twice has the same effect as once). Or ask a human to approve before they run. Some errors should end the loop, not become a message.

**3. Agents that call other agents.** Each inner agent may get its own step count. So the total work can be much bigger than any one limit suggests. Set a budget for the whole run, not just each piece. Also watch for the same tool call repeating, and stop early when you see it.

judge.notes: No check fails. Minor: each point runs past the requested two or three sentences, and the checkpoint idea comes from outside the lesson, though it doesn't contradict it.

learn:term.q: How is “hard step limit” different from “recursion limit”?
learn:term.a:
They are the same safety idea. One is the general name, the other is LangGraph's name for it.

**Hard step limit** is the concept. An agent is a loop, and you cap how many times it can go around. When it hits the cap, it stops, even with no final answer. In the plain loop, `MAX_STEPS` is that cap.

**Recursion limit** is how LangGraph sets that cap. "Recursion" here just means the graph running step after step. You pass it as `recursion_limit` when you call the graph:

```python
graph.invoke({"messages": messages}, config={"recursion_limit": 25})
```

Two things to know about LangGraph's version:

- **It counts in its own units.** A model call is one step. That call's tool runs together are another. So `25` allows about 12 rounds.
- **Its default is far too high.** It is about 10,000 steps. A stuck agent could spend money for a long time. So always set your own small number.

When the limit is reached, LangGraph raises `GraphRecursionError`.

An everyday comparison: "a time limit" is the idea. The number you type into a kitchen timer is the actual setting.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Delete it, since its source has changed”?
check:0:1.a:
"Delete it" gets one thing right. A version mismatch means you can't trust the fact as it stands. Using it as if nothing happened would be a mistake, and deleting at least avoids that.

But it treats "stale" as "wrong", and the lesson says stale means "check again". A new version only tells you the source changed *somehow*. Maybe the refund limit moved. Or maybe someone fixed a typo elsewhere in that policy row, and the $100 rule is still true. You can't tell without looking.

Deleting also throws away useful things. The saved fact holds its `source`, like `main.hr.policies/12`. That's a pointer telling you exactly where to re-check. Once it's gone, the agent has nothing to refresh and has simply forgotten. The next time a refund comes up, it may guess, or start from scratch.

Re-reading the source, then refreshing or replacing the fact, is better because it swaps the uncertain fact for the current truth, rather than trading it for no knowledge at all. If the re-read fails, the agent can still honestly say "I can't confirm that right now."

check:0:2.q: Why not “Use it, since most changes don't affect it”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. Many changes to a source really don't touch the fact you saved. The policy row might have changed a typo or an unrelated field, and the refund rule could still be true.

The problem is that the agent can't know that without looking. The version number only says "something changed." It doesn't say what. If the agent guesses "probably fine," it is back to the original problem: repeating a rule with full confidence when it might be out of date. That is exactly what saving versions was meant to prevent.

Also, guessing wrong costs a lot. A customer could get told the wrong refund rule. Re-reading one row costs very little.

Remember, stale means "check again," not "wrong" and not "fine." This option treats it as "fine," which skips the check entirely.

"Re-read the source, then refresh or replace it" is better because it turns an unknown into a known. You look at what the source says now, then either confirm the fact or save the new version, so the agent only states what it has actually checked.

judge.notes: No real problems; the cost claims (a wrong rule costs a lot, re-reading one row is cheap) go beyond the lesson but don't contradict it.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Delete it, since it may be out of date”?
check:1:1.a:
"Delete it" comes from a good instinct. Memories really can go out of date, and the lesson warns that an agent can repeat an old rule with full confidence. Being careful is right.

But here, the check has already answered the question. The fact was saved from the sites page at version 7. The sites page is still at version 7. The source hasn't changed since the fact was saved, so the fact is **fresh**. There's nothing to fix.

Deleting it would throw away a good fact for no reason. The agent would then have to re-read the source or say "I can't confirm that", even though it could confirm it with one simple comparison.

Also, deleting is the wrong move even when a fact *is* stale. Stale means "check again", not "wrong". You re-read the source and refresh the fact. You don't erase it.

"Use it, since the fact is still fresh" is better because the matching versions are exactly the evidence the agent needs to trust the fact.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Ask a model if the fact is still true”?
check:1:2.a:
**Why not "Ask a model if the fact is still true"?**

It gets one thing right: checking a memory before trusting it is a good habit. That is the whole point of this lesson.

But here, the check is already done, and it needs no model. The fact was saved from the sites page at version 7. The sites page is still at version 7. A **version** is a number that goes up each time the source changes. Same number means the source hasn't changed since the fact was saved. The lesson says to make this comparison in plain code, with no model call. A simple `!=` check settles it.

Asking a model adds an extra step that this case doesn't need. The lesson saves model checks for a different situation: when something changed but no source got a new version, like a user saying "I moved to York". That is the hard case. This isn't it.

**What makes the right answer better:** "Use it, since the fact is still fresh" is better because the saved version matches the source's version now, so plain code has already shown the fact is fresh.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Delete it at the end of each chat”?
check:2:0.a:
"Delete it at the end of each chat" gets one thing right. A deleted fact can never go out of date without anyone noticing, because it is gone.

But it misses the point of **long-term memory**, which is memory that keeps facts between chats. If every chat-sourced fact is wiped when the chat ends, the agent has no long-term memory for those facts at all. Next time, the user has to tell it everything again, including things that are still true.

So deleting doesn't manage staleness. It just throws away the memory.

The right answer is "Give it an expiry date." An **expiry date** is a saved date after which the fact no longer counts as fresh. It does for chat facts what the version check does for facts with a source: it tells the agent when to check again.

What makes it better: the fact stays usable across chats until its expiry date, and after that the agent knows to confirm it instead of trusting it forever.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Ask the user to confirm it every time”?
check:2:1.a:
Asking the user gets one thing right. For a fact that came from chat, the user *is* the source. So asking them is a real way to re-check it, and it does stop the fact going stale without anyone noticing.

The problem is "every time". Memory exists so the agent doesn't have to ask again. If every use of "has a dog named Max" starts with "Is that still true?", the memory is barely saving anything. It also costs the user an extra step each time, and that adds up fast.

It can backfire, too. People who get asked the same thing over and over start saying "yes" without reading. Then a stale fact gets confirmed anyway, and you've lost the safety you wanted.

It also treats a fact saved five minutes ago the same as one saved two years ago. Those don't carry the same risk.

**Give it an expiry date** is better because the agent uses the fact freely while it's recent, and only re-checks with the user once it's old enough to doubt.

judge.notes: No real problems. The point about users clicking 'yes' without reading goes beyond the lesson, but it doesn't contradict it.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Save the row's version, not the table's” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
A Delta table keeps a **table version**: a counter that goes up after every write to the table. Any write counts. Adding a row, fixing a typo in another row, or running `OPTIMIZE` (a cleanup job that repacks files and changes no data) all bump it.

So if you save the table's version with a fact, the check breaks. The next unrelated write makes every saved fact look stale.

**A small example.** Your agent saved "refunds over $100 need a manager" from row 12 of `main.hr.policies`. The table was at version 40. Overnight, someone edits row 30, the parking policy. A nightly `OPTIMIZE` also runs. The table is now at version 42, but row 12 never changed.

With the table's version, every memory looks stale. The agent re-reads every source or says "I can't confirm that right now" over and over. That wastes time and annoys users. Worse, people learn that "stale" means nothing, so they ignore the warnings.

With the **row's version** (`_metadata.row_commit_version`), the check only fires when row 12 itself is inserted, updated or merged. A stale warning then means something really did change.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Compare versions, sort into three lists” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
Here's a 30-second answer you could say out loud.

**The problem.** "An agent's long-term memory keeps facts between chats. But when the source changes, like a refund policy, the saved fact doesn't. So the agent repeats the old rule with full confidence."

**The idea.** "I save each fact with its source and that source's version: a number that goes up on every change. Before using a fact, I compare the saved version with the current one in plain code, with no model call. If they match, it's fresh. If they differ, it's stale. That means 're-check', not 'delete'. If there's no current version to compare, it goes in a separate 'unknown' list, because 'can't tell' isn't 'fresh'."

**The edge case.** "This only catches source changes. If a user says 'I moved to York', no version changes, so 'lives in Leeds' still looks fresh. Catching that needs a model, and models are still weak at it."

**Likely follow-up:** "In Databricks, why use the row's version, not the table's?"

**Hint:** A row is one record, like policy 12. The table's version goes up on every write to any row. So every fact would look stale all the time.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs to watch for**

- **Old rules after an update.** Right after a policy changes, users start correcting the agent. It quotes the old rule with full confidence. In the trace (the step-by-step record of a run), the memory is used, but no version comparison happens first.
- **Stale count is always zero.** Over weeks, nothing is ever flagged. Either the check isn't running or versions were never saved with the facts.
- **Almost everything is stale.** One edit anywhere in the table flags many facts. You are probably reading the table's version, not the row's.
- **Unknown is always empty.** Facts from chat exist, but none land in unknown. They are being counted as fresh.
- **Memories quietly disappear.** The fact count drops after source updates. Stale facts are being deleted instead of re-checked.
- **Tests look perfect.** Your test data never changes, so nothing can go stale.

**Quickest check**

In a test setup, edit one source row so its version goes up. Then ask the agent about that fact. It should flag the fact as stale and re-read the source. Then it should give the new rule or say "I can't confirm that right now". Edit a different row too. Facts from untouched rows should stay fresh.

judge.notes: No major problems. It runs to about 205 words, slightly over the target, and it leaves out the lesson's known blind spot (a user-stated change like 'moved to York' that looks fresh), but nothing in it is wrong.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where the version check needs extra care.

**1. The version goes up for a change that doesn't matter.**
A row's version rises on any edit to that row, even a typo fix in another column. Every memory tied to it then looks stale, so the agent keeps re-checking. Also save a **hash** of the exact text you relied on. A hash is a short fingerprint that changes only when the text changes. If the version moved but the hash matches, refresh the saved version and carry on.

**2. The source disappears or gets rebuilt.**
The row might be deleted, or the whole table rewritten so row ids and versions start over. A missing version must not count as "matches". Put these facts in unknown, re-find the source, and say "I can't confirm that right now" if you can't.

**3. You have thousands of memories.**
Asking the database once per fact gets slow. Gather all the sources you need first. Fetch their versions in one query. Then walk through the memories once, comparing each against that lookup table.

judge.notes: No criterion fails, but the answer leaves out the lesson's own main limit: a change with no new source version (like 'I moved to York') still looks fresh, and unversioned facts need an expiry date.

learn:term.a:
The **source** is *where* a fact came from. The **version** is *which edition* of that source it came from.

Think of a recipe you copied from a cookbook. The source is the book and page number. The version is the edition. If a new edition comes out, the page is still the same place, but the recipe on it may have changed.

A fact's source stays the same. It's the address you go back to. The version is a number that goes up each time that source is edited. Saving both says: "I learned this from here, when it was at this edition."

They work as a pair. The source tells your code where to look now. The version tells it whether anything changed since you saved the fact.

In the lesson's table, the refund fact came from `policy` at version 3. The policy is now at 4, so the fact is stale: re-read it. The office fact came from `sites` at 7, still 7, so it's fresh. The pet fact came from `chat`, which has no version, so it's unknown.

In the code, the source is `"main.hr.policies/12"` and the version is `3`.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Both 1.0: the tools were right”?
check:0:0.a:
"Both 1.0" gets one thing right. The tool selection score really is 1.0. Every step called the correct tool, in the correct order, so that level is perfect.

What it misses is that there are two separate scores, and they check different things. The arguments score asks a stricter question: was it the right tool *and* the right arguments? Arguments are the values you pass into a tool, like `order_id` or `amount`. One wrong argument means that call fails the stricter check. So the arguments score drops below 1.0.

The lesson's example shows this. The agent called `lookup_order` and `refund`, both correct. But it passed `amount=25` instead of `amount=250`. Tool selection is 2/2 = 1.0. Arguments are 1/2 = 0.5. That refund would cost a real customer money, even though the agent "picked the right tools."

Scoring both levels as 1.0 would hide exactly the kind of mistake this lesson is about.

"Tool selection 1.0, arguments below 1.0" is better because it shows the tools were right while still catching the bad argument.

check:0:2.a:
"Both below 1.0" gets one thing right. The arguments score does drop. One call had a wrong argument, so not every call is fully correct.

But it misses how the two scores are built. **Tool selection** only asks one question: was the right tool called at each step? It looks at tool names and nothing else. In this question, every name matched, in the right order. So tool selection is a perfect 1.0.

The wrong argument only shows up in the **arguments** score. That score asks for the right tool *and* the right arguments. Think of the lesson's example. `refund(order_id="A-1", amount=25)` picked the right tool, so it still counts for tool selection. It only fails the arguments check, because 25 is not 250. That gives tool selection 2/2 = 1.0 and arguments 1/2 = 0.5.

That split is the whole point of scoring two levels. It tells you *where* the agent went wrong. Here the agent chose its tools well and slipped on a value.

"Tool selection 1.0, arguments below 1.0" is better because a bad argument can only lower the score that actually checks arguments.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Ignore it, as the first two match”?
check:1:1.a:
"Ignore it" gets one thing right. The first two calls really do match, so the agent deserves credit for them.

What it misses is that the third call is not harmless. It is a second `refund`. In the real world, that customer gets paid twice, and the business loses money. An agent that does extra actions can cause damage just as much as one that skips a step.

If the score ignores extra calls, an agent could spam calls and still look perfect. You would never see the problem in your test results, only later in production (the live system real users touch).

Dividing by the length of the longer list fixes this. Here the expected list has 2 calls and the actual list has 3. So you divide by 3, and the scores become 2/3 for tool selection and 2/3 for arguments. The extra call drags the score down, like a wrong answer written on a test.

"Count it as a wrong call" is better because it makes the score reflect what the agent actually did, including actions it should never have taken.

judge.notes: No real problems. Minor: the 2/3 arguments figure assumes the first two calls' arguments match, which the question doesn't state, and the lesson compares an extra call to a 'blank' answer rather than a 'wrong' one.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Count it as right, refund was expected”?
check:1:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. `refund` really is a tool the task needed. So the agent didn't pick a strange tool out of nowhere.

But the expected list has only one `refund`. The agent's first `refund` already matched it. The second `refund` has nothing in the expected list to line up with, because the scorer compares by position: first with first, second with second, third with third. In third place, the expected list is empty. An empty slot can't be matched, so that call scores as wrong.

It also matters in the real world. A second refund means the customer gets paid twice. "Refund was expected" asks whether that kind of call ever shows up. The real question is whether this exact call belonged in this exact spot.

That's why the scorer divides by the longer list. Here that's 3 calls, so the tool score is 2/3, not a perfect 1.0. The extra call drags the score down, the same way a missing call would.

"Count it as a wrong call" is better because an extra action is a real mistake that can cause real damage, so the score should show it.

judge.notes: No real problems; the 2/3 tool score and the position-by-position reasoning match the lesson. The 'customer gets paid twice' point is a small inference beyond the lesson, but a reasonable one.

check:2:0.q: Why not “The agent's last message to the user”?
check:2:0.a:
The agent's last message is what the agent *says* happened. It is not proof of what *did* happen.

It does get one thing right. It shows what the user was told, and that matters. A confusing or rude reply is a real problem worth catching.

But it misses the actual outcome. An agent can write "Your order is cancelled" when:

- the `cancel` call failed with an error the agent ignored,
- it cancelled the wrong order because of a bad `order_id` argument,
- it never made the call at all and just claimed it did.

In all three cases the message looks fine. Yet the order is still active. Checking the message means trusting the agent's own report, and the whole point of the test is to avoid trusting it.

This is why benchmarks like tau-bench check the **final state**. "Final state" means what the system looks like after the task is done, such as the rows in a database.

Checking the order's row in the database is better because it looks at what actually changed, no matter what the agent's calls or messages claimed.

check:2:1.q: Why not “The number of tool calls it made”?
check:2:1.a:
Counting the calls tells you how busy the agent was. It doesn't tell you what the agent actually did.

It does get one thing right. If the agent made far more or far fewer calls than your reference, that's a hint something went off track. But it's only a hint.

Here's what it misses:

- **Same count, wrong outcome.** The agent could make exactly the expected number of calls and still never cancel the order. Maybe it called the wrong tool, or passed the wrong `order_id`.
- **Different count, right outcome.** The question says the calls differ a little from your reference. The agent might have taken an extra lookup step and still cancelled the order correctly. A count would flag that as a problem when it isn't one.

Either way, the number answers "how many?" when your real question is "did the order end up cancelled?"

**The order's row in the database** is the better answer. It checks the final state, meaning what's actually true after the task. That tells you directly whether the order really ended up cancelled, however the agent got there.

judge.notes: No significant problems; it runs close to the 200-word limit and spends a few sentences on the database row where one was asked for.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Compare the lists side by side” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer:**

*The problem:* "An agent can call the right tool with the wrong argument. A refund of 25 instead of 250 looks fine if you only check tool names, but it did real damage."

*The idea:* "So I score two levels. I line up the expected calls and the actual calls by position: first with first, second with second. A matching name counts toward tool selection. A matching name *and* matching arguments counts toward argument correctness. I divide by the longer list's length, so a missing or extra call counts as wrong, like a blank answer on a test. It's plain code, so there's no LLM judge (a model grading another model's output) to disagree with."

*The trade-off:* "Matching by position is strict. If the agent adds one harmless extra call early, every later call shifts one place and looks wrong, even when the work was fine."

**A likely follow-up:** "What if the order of calls doesn't matter?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Say you'd match calls by content instead of position for order-free steps. Or you'd check the **final state** (the result left behind, like the database after the task), the way tau-bench does.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs this went wrong**

- **The two scores always match.** If tool selection and arguments are identical on every run, the scorer is probably only checking tool names. A wrong amount, like 25 instead of 250, slips through.
- **Scores look great but users complain.** Evals say the agent is fine. Then real refunds come out wrong, or orders get looked up twice. The traces (the step-by-step log of each tool call) show bad arguments that nothing flagged.
- **Short runs score perfectly.** An agent that stops after one correct call still gets 1.0. That means missing calls aren't counted as wrong. The scorer is dividing by the shorter list instead of the longer one.
- **Extra calls cost nothing.** An agent that calls `refund` three times scores the same as one that calls it once.
- **Only the final answer is judged.** The agent's reply sounds right, so it passes, even though the calls behind it were wrong.

**Quickest check**

Build two tiny test cases by hand. In the first, copy the lesson's refund example with 25 instead of 250. In the second, drop one expected call entirely. Run your scorer on both. You should see tool selection stay high while arguments drop, and the missing call should pull both scores down.

judge.notes: No real problems. At about 210 words it is slightly over the 200-word guide, and 'Evals' is not explained.

learn:stops.a:
**Situation 1: more than one valid path.** Some tasks can be done correctly in different orders, or with a harmless extra lookup. Comparing first with first, second with second will mark those runs wrong. One early extra call also shifts every later call out of line, so everything after it looks wrong too. Instead, compare calls as an unordered set where order truly doesn't matter, or check the **final state** (what the database looks like afterwards), as tau-bench does.

**Situation 2: free-text arguments.** IDs and amounts should match exactly. A search query like "refund policy" versus "policy for refunds" means the same thing but fails an exact match. Use exact checks for fields like `order_id` and `amount`. For text fields, clean them up first (lowercase, trim spaces) or use a looser comparison. This could be an LLM judge, which means another model grading the answer.

**Situation 3: no reference exists.** Real user traffic has no list of expected calls. Here you can check outcomes and safety rules instead, such as "never refund more than the order total." You can also label a small sample by hand to create new reference tasks.

judge.notes: No real problems; Situations 1 and 2 run four to five sentences each, over the two-to-three guideline, but the answer is about 190 words and consistent with the lesson.

learn:term.a:
**Tool selection** asks one simple question at each step: did the agent pick the right tool? It ignores what the agent passed into that tool.

**An everyday comparison.** You ask a helper to hang a picture. Step one, they grab the tape measure. Step two, they grab the drill. Those are the right tools, so tool selection is perfect. Whether they drilled the hole in the right spot is a separate question. That second question is the "arguments" level.

**In the lesson's example**, the agent made two calls:

- It called `lookup_order` when `lookup_order` was expected. Right tool.
- It called `refund` when `refund` was expected. Right tool.

So tool selection is 2 out of 2, which is `1.0`. That is a perfect score, even though the refund used `amount=25` instead of `amount=250`. That mistake shows up only in the arguments score. (Arguments are the values handed to a tool, like `order_id` or `amount`.)

The two scores are kept separate for a reason. A perfect tool selection score can hide a costly mistake.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The model ignores the gap and carries on”?
check:0:0.a:
It's a natural guess. Models often cope with messy or incomplete text, so it feels like they'd shrug off a missing piece too. That instinct is fair for ordinary chat messages.

But a missing tool result isn't messy text. It's a broken structure. Every tool call has an `id`, and the API (the service you send the chat to) expects a later message with a matching `tool_call_id`. Before the model reads anything, the API checks that every call has its answer.

If one is missing, the request is refused right there. The model never sees the chat, so it never gets the chance to "ignore" the gap. You get an error back instead of a reply.

That's why the lesson says to send the crash as the result. An error message still counts as an answer to the call. In LangGraph, `ToolNode(tools, handle_tool_errors=True)` does this for you.

"The API rejects the whole request" is better because the check happens before the model runs, and it fails the entire chat, not just the one gap.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The tool is called again automatically”?
check:0:2.a:
That answer has a reasonable instinct behind it. A crash feels like something a system should recover from, and retrying is a common fix in software. Some frameworks even let you set up retries on purpose.

But nothing retries by default here. The model's service never runs your tools. It only reads the conversation you send it. Your own code, or a helper like LangGraph's `ToolNode`, does the actual running.

So on the next model call, the service just looks at the history. It sees a tool call with id `call_1`. Then it looks for a message with `tool_call_id` set to `call_1`, and there isn't one. That is a dangling tool call, meaning a call that never got an answer. The service doesn't guess what happened, and it doesn't re-run anything. It refuses the request.

That's why the lesson says to send the error as the result. Setting `handle_tool_errors=True` on `ToolNode` does this for you, so every call still gets a reply.

"The API rejects the whole request" is the better answer because the service checks that every call has a matching result, and a missing one makes the entire chat invalid.

judge.notes: Minor: the claims that the service never runs tools and that some frameworks offer retries come from outside the lesson, but nothing contradicts it.

check:1:1.q: Why not “The name of the model”?
check:1:1.a:
The model's name feels like a natural label. A result does need to say where it belongs. But the model's name doesn't do that job.

**What it misses:** the name is the same for every call in the chat. A model can make several tool calls in one turn, say `call_7` for `search` and `call_8` for a weather lookup. If each result only said "from model X", nothing would show which result answers which call. The service (the model provider's system that checks your messages) matches results to calls by id, not by name.

Also, the result message isn't really "about" the model. It answers one specific request. The `role: 'tool'` field already says it's a tool result. The id says which call it answers.

```python
{'role': 'tool', 'tool_call_id': 'call_7', 'content': '...'}
```

Without `tool_call_id`, `call_7` stays unanswered. That's a dangling tool call, and the service rejects the whole chat.

**Why "The id call_7" is better:** the id is the one detail that ties this exact result to this exact call, so the service can confirm every call got its answer.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The time the search ended”?
check:1:2.a:
A finish time sounds useful. It tells you *when* something happened, and that can help when you read logs later. Logs are the running notes your program writes about what it did.

But the model's service doesn't use time to match anything. It looks at each result and asks one question: "Which call does this answer?" A timestamp can't tell it that. Two searches could finish at the same moment. Or they could finish in a different order than they started. Either way, the service would have no way to know which result goes with which call.

So if your result carries only a time, `call_7` still looks unanswered. That is a dangling tool call, and the service rejects the whole chat.

The id is what links the two messages together:

```python
{'role': 'tool', 'tool_call_id': 'call_7', 'content': '...'}
```

You can still record the time somewhere else if you like. It just can't replace the id.

"The id call_7" is better because the id is the one thing the service uses to pair each result with the exact call it answers.

check:2:0.q: Why not “The trim kept too few messages”?
check:2:0.a:
It points at the right place. The trim is the cause. But it blames the wrong thing about the trim.

Model APIs don't reject a chat for being short. A conversation with just two or three messages is perfectly fine. So keeping "too few" messages can't, by itself, cause a rejection. At worst, the model forgets some older context and gives a weaker answer. That is a quality problem, not an error.

What the API checks is pairing. Every tool call has an `id`, and a tool result must reference that `id` through its `tool_call_id`. If the trim cuts between the two, one half is left alone. Say the trim drops the assistant message with `call_1` but keeps the message with `'tool_call_id': 'call_1'`. Now a result answers a call that isn't there. Or the trim keeps the call and drops its result. That is a dangling tool call. Either way, the API rejects the request.

So the issue is *where* the cut lands, not *how much* it removes.

"The trim split a tool call from its result" is better because it names the exact rule the API enforces: every call needs its matching result.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that an orphaned result is also rejected goes slightly beyond the lesson, which only states the dangling-call case, but it does not contradict it. The length is just under 200 words.

check:2:1.q: Why not “The trim removed the system prompt”?
check:2:1.a:
Dropping the system prompt is a real risk when you trim. The system prompt is the first message that tells the model how to behave. Good trimming code should always keep it, so this option points at a genuine thing to guard against.

But it doesn't match the symptom. Without a system prompt, the request is still a valid conversation. The model API (the service you send the chat to) usually accepts it. The model just acts differently. It might forget its rules or its tone. You would see odd answers, not rejected requests.

Look at the word "some" too. A trim that drops the system prompt would likely do it the same way every time. Rejections that hit only some requests suggest the problem depends on exactly where the cut lands.

A rejection means the chat broke a structural rule. One such rule is that every tool call needs a matching result, and every result needs its call. If the cut falls between a call and its result, one half is left alone, and the API refuses the whole chat.

"The trim split a tool call from its result" is better because it explains both an outright rejection and why only some requests fail.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. The 'some requests' argument is a bit speculative, since trimming only happens on long chats either way, and the answer runs right at the ~200-word limit.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Don't use a mutable default argument” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
A **default argument** is the value a function uses when the caller leaves that input out. **Mutable** means the value can be changed in place, like a list you can append to.

Python builds a default value once, when the function is defined. It does not build a fresh one on each call. So a default list is shared by every call that relies on it.

```python
def add_message(msg, history=[]):
    history.append(msg)
    return history

chat_a = add_message("Hi from Ana")
chat_b = add_message("Hi from Ben")
print(chat_b)  # ['Hi from Ana', 'Hi from Ben']
```

Ben's "new" chat already holds Ana's message. Both names point at the same list.

In real chat code, this means separate conversations quietly merge. One user's messages, tool calls and tool results show up in another user's chat. That can leak private data. It also gives the model confusing context. And the shared list grows with every conversation, so the history keeps getting longer.

The fix is to default to `None` and make a new list inside the function:

```python
def add_message(msg, history=None):
    if history is None:
        history = []
    history.append(msg)
    return history
```

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “A waiting list of open calls” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* Every tool call from the model gets an id. Each call needs a tool result that names that id. If even one call has no result, the model's service rejects the whole chat. This often happens after trimming old messages, or when a tool crashes.

*The idea:* I keep a list called `waiting`. When I see a tool call, I add its id. When I see a result, I remove the id it answers. It's like a coat check: each ticket waits until its coat is collected. Whatever is left at the end is a dangling call, meaning a call that never got a result. Those ids are already in the order the calls were made.

*Edge case:* A result might name an id that was never called, perhaps because trimming removed the call. I'd flag that too, not quietly ignore it.

**Likely follow-up:** "How would you stop dangling calls from happening at all?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Never let a crash go silent. Send the error back as the tool's result. In LangGraph, `ToolNode` with `handle_tool_errors=True` does this. Also, when trimming history, keep or drop each call together with its result.

judge.notes: The orphan-result edge case goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it. The answer is about 197 words, just under the limit.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Spotting dangling tool calls**

A missing result rarely fails quietly. The model's service rejects the whole chat. So the signs are loud, but they show up only at certain moments.

**Warning signs**

- **Short tests pass, long chats fail.** Early on, nothing gets trimmed (cut from the history to save space). Later, trimming can drop a tool result but keep its call.
- **Failures follow a tool error.** If a tool crashes and no result is sent, the next request to the model is rejected. With LangGraph's `ToolNode` on its default setting, a crashing tool stops the run instead.
- **The error points at the conversation, not your logic.** The rejection is about the shape of the message list, not about a wrong answer.

**Quickest check**

Look at the exact message list that was sent when it failed. For each `tool_calls` entry on an assistant message, find a `tool` message whose `tool_call_id` matches that call's `id`. Any call without a match is your dangling call. Then ask whether trimming removed its result or a crash skipped it.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where the simple rule needs extra care.

**1. Trimming a long chat.** If you cut old messages to save space, you can cut a call but keep its result, or the reverse. Either way the service rejects the chat. Trim in whole groups instead: keep or drop a tool call together with all of its results.

**2. Several calls at once.** A model can ask for many tools in one message. This is called "parallel tool calls." Results may come back in a different order. Match by `id`, never by position. Make sure every call in that message has its result before the model speaks again.

**3. Switching model providers.** A provider is the company whose model service you call. Each one shapes messages a little differently. For example, one uses `tool_call_id`, while another puts results in a `user` message as a `tool_result` block with a `tool_use_id`. Convert everything to one shape first, then check for dangling calls.

In all three cases, keep the same idea. Every call gets exactly one answer. If a tool crashes or times out, send the error as its result.

judge.notes: Nothing contradicts the lesson. The orphan-result rejection, the 'exactly one answer' wording and the provider formats go beyond what the lesson states, but they are accurate.

learn:term.q: What does “dangling tool call” mean here?
learn:term.a:
A **dangling tool call** is a tool call that never got an answer.

Think of a coat check. You hand over your coat and get ticket 12. If nobody ever comes back with ticket 12, that ticket is left "dangling." It's an open promise that was never closed.

In the lesson's example, the assistant message makes a call with the id `call_1`. That's the ticket. The next message has `role: 'tool'` and `tool_call_id: 'call_1'`. That's the coat being collected. The result points back to the call's id, so the pair is complete.

Now imagine the second message is missing:

```python
{'role': 'assistant', 'tool_calls': [{'id': 'call_1', 'name': 'search'}]}
# no message with tool_call_id 'call_1'
```

Now `call_1` is dangling. The model's service (the API, the online system you send the chat to) will reject the whole conversation.

This usually happens in two ways. Trimming old history can cut off the result. Or a tool crashes and sends nothing back. The fix for a crash is to send the error message as the result, so the call still gets an answer.

check:0:0.q: Why not “A bigger model, so it reads the names more care…”?
check:0:0.a:
A bigger model is not a silly idea. Larger models are often better at following instructions. So it might help a little.

But it misses the real cause. The model picks a tool only by reading each tool's name, description and parameters. If `get_data` has a vague description like "Gets data", it looks like it could answer anything. A bigger model reads that same vague text. It still has to guess.

It is also not cheap. A bigger model usually costs more for every request and answers more slowly. You would pay that price on every call, forever, to work around a few unclear sentences.

Remember that the tool descriptions are part of your prompt. On Databricks, `UCFunctionToolkit` builds those descriptions from the comments on your Unity Catalog function and its parameters. Fixing a comment takes a minute. It costs nothing to run, and it fixes the problem where it starts.

**Why "Clearer function and parameter comments" is better:** it gives the model the information it was missing, so even the current model can tell `lookup_order` apart from `get_data`, at almost no cost.

judge.notes: Passes. The cost and speed claims about bigger models go beyond the lesson but don't contradict it. Minor wobble: 'costs nothing to run' vs 'almost no cost'.

check:0:2.q: Why not “More tools, so the right one is easier to find”?
check:0:2.a:
It's a natural idea. If the model can't find the right tool, giving it more options sounds helpful. And sometimes a missing tool really is the problem.

But here, the right tool already exists. `lookup_order` is there. The model just isn't choosing it. Remember how it chooses: it reads each tool's name, description and parameters, then picks the best match. If it keeps grabbing `get_data`, the descriptions aren't telling the two apart clearly.

Adding more tools doesn't fix that. It gives the model more descriptions to read and compare, which means more chances to mix them up. A vague name like `get_data` can still look like a match for almost anything.

It's also not cheap. Each new tool is a new Unity Catalog function to write, test and set permissions on. Permissions are the rules for who is allowed to run it.

"Clearer function and parameter comments" is better because `UCFunctionToolkit` turns those comments into the descriptions the model reads, so a quick edit to the comments directly fixes the confusing part of the prompt.

check:1:0.q: Why not “A longer system prompt in each agent”?
check:1:0.a:
A **system prompt** is the standing set of instructions the model reads before every conversation. Making it longer feels helpful, and it gets one thing right: wording matters. The lesson says tool descriptions are part of the prompt, so clear text does help the model pick the right tool.

But it doesn't fix the two real problems in the question.

First, there are still three separate copies of the "find customer" tool. A longer prompt doesn't merge them. Each team still maintains its own version, and they can drift apart. You would also be copying the extra prompt text into three agents, which adds even more duplication.

Second, nobody controls who can run the tool. A prompt is just words to the model. It can ask the model to behave, but it can't enforce anything. It can't stop a person or another agent from calling the tool. Permissions have to live in the platform, not in the instructions.

"One Unity Catalog function, shared by all" is better because it gives one governed copy with real permission control, and `UCFunctionToolkit` lets every team's agent use it as a tool.

check:1:2.q: Why not “A shared file in one team's code folder”?
check:1:2.a:
A shared file gets one thing right. It fixes the copying problem. Instead of three teams each writing their own "find customer" tool, there is one version. That's **reuse**, and reuse is good.

But the question has a second problem: nobody controls who can run the tool. Moving the code into one team's folder doesn't change that. The file is still just code inside agents, with no rule about who may run it.

Unity Catalog functions cover both problems. They are **reusable**, so every team can use the same one. They are **governed**, meaning managed under shared rules in one central place. And they are **permissioned**, meaning you choose which people or groups are allowed to run them. Each team can then load the function with `UCFunctionToolkit`, which turns it into a LangChain tool. It uses the function's comments as the tool's description.

"One Unity Catalog function, shared by all" is better because it keeps the reuse of a shared file and adds the control over who can run it that the file lacks.

judge.notes: No hard failure. The claim that a shared file in one team's folder gives real reuse is an assumption the lesson doesn't support, and the UCFunctionToolkit detail is tangential.

check:2:1.a:
It's a natural guess. The whole message does contain what the tool needs, since "A-1042" is in there. So the instinct to pass along the user's words isn't silly.

But the whole message is what the **model** reads, not what the **tool** receives. The tool's schema says exactly what it accepts: one parameter, `order_id`, a string described as "The order number, like A-1042". When the model calls the tool, it fills in that parameter and nothing else.

Think about what the tool does with its input. `lookup_order` is a Unity Catalog function. It likely searches a table for a matching order number. If you hand it "Where is my parcel? My order is A-1042.", no order has that number, so the lookup fails.

Pulling the order number out of messy human text is the model's job. That's the point of giving it a clear schema. The tool stays simple and only deals with clean inputs.

So the call looks like this:

```json
{"order_id": "A-1042"}
```

"order_id set to A-1042" is right because the model sends only the arguments the schema asks for, already extracted and in the expected shape.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that the tool searches a table and fails on the full message is an inference beyond the lesson, but it is hedged with 'likely'.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Nothing, the tool finds it”?
check:2:2.a:
"Nothing, the tool finds it" gets one thing right. The tool does the real lookup work. Once it has an order number, it goes to the database and finds the status and delivery date. The model does not do that part.

What it misses is that the tool cannot see the chat. It never reads the user's message. It only gets the inputs the model hands it. Those inputs are called **arguments**: the actual values filled into the tool's parameters.

The tool schema says `lookup_order` takes one parameter, `order_id`, and lists it under `required`. That means the tool will not run without it. So the model's job is to read "My order is A-1042," match it to the parameter's description ("The order number, like A-1042"), and pull out the value.

What the model sends looks like this:

```json
{"order_id": "A-1042"}
```

If it sent nothing, the tool would have no idea which order to look up.

"`order_id` set to A-1042" is better because the model reads the schema, takes the value from the user's words, and passes it in as the required argument, which is the only way the tool learns what to look up.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Fill the inside, then wrap it” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem.** "A chat model picks a tool by reading its schema: a name, a description and the inputs it takes. On Databricks, those facts live in a Unity Catalog function. So I need to reshape that function into the nested format the model expects."

**The idea.** "I build the innermost part first. I go through the parameters once. For each one, I translate the database type into the model's word using a lookup table, and attach its comment. Once that inner part is complete, I wrap it in the `parameters` layer, then the `"function"` layer, then the outer layer. It's like packing boxes inside boxes."

**A trade-off.** "The descriptions come straight from the function's comments. If a comment is empty or vague, the model may pick the wrong tool. So the schema is only as good as the comments behind it."

**A likely follow-up**

*"What happens if a parameter's type isn't in your lookup table?"*

Hint: a strong answer says you'd fail with a clear error rather than quietly guess. A wrong type would mislead the model, and that kind of bug is hard to spot later.

judge.notes: No real problems. The follow-up hint (fail with a clear error on an unknown type) goes beyond the lesson but does not contradict it. The answer is about 195 words, just under the limit.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The model picks the wrong tool, or no tool at all.** It might answer from memory instead of calling `lookup_order`. This often means the description is vague or empty.
- **Bad inputs.** The model sends `1042` when your function expects `"A-1042"`. Missing parameter comments or a wrong type leave it guessing the format.
- **Missing-input errors.** A call fails because an input was left out. That can mean `required` does not list it.
- **Great in testing, worse with real users.** Your test prompts may name the tool almost word for word, so it works. Real users phrase things loosely, and a weak description stops matching.
- **Blank descriptions after `UCFunctionToolkit`.** The toolkit copies the function and parameter comments. If you never wrote those comments in Unity Catalog, the model gets nothing to read.

**Quickest check**

Print the tools that `UCFunctionToolkit` produced. Read each one as if you were the model: the name, the description, and every parameter's type and comment. Ask yourself: "With only this text, would I know when to call it and what to pass?" If not, fix the comments on the Unity Catalog function. The model can only use what is written there.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where this needs extra care.

**1. Lots of tools.** With a few tools, the model picks well. With dozens, descriptions start to overlap and the model grabs the wrong one. Every schema is also sent with every request, so your prompt grows. Keep each agent's tool list short. Make each description clearly different. Or split the work across smaller agents, each with its own tools.

**2. Missing or vague comments.** `UCFunctionToolkit` uses your function and parameter comments as the descriptions. If a comment is empty or says "id", the model has to guess. Write comments as if they were prompt text: say what the tool does, when to use it, and give an example input.

**3. The function changes later.** Someone renames a parameter or changes what the function returns. The schema updates, but the agent's behaviour may shift without anyone noticing. Keep a small set of test questions. Re-run them with MLflow evaluation (scoring the agent's answers against expected ones) after any change to a tool.

judge.notes: Minor: MLflow evaluation is not in the lesson, and 'the schema updates' glosses over the fact that the toolkit only rebuilds the schema when it is re-created. Neither contradicts the lesson.

learn:term.a:
Both are part of the tool schema, and the model reads both when picking a tool. They just do different jobs.

**The name** is a short label for the tool. In the lesson's example it's `lookup_order`. It's compact, with no spaces, and it tells the model at a glance roughly what the tool is about.

**The description** is a plain sentence that spells out what the tool does: "Look up an order's status and delivery date." It adds detail the name can't fit, like *what* you get back.

Think of a restaurant menu. Each dish has a name, like "Pad Thai," and a line underneath: "rice noodles, peanuts, lime." You read both to decide what to order. The name catches your eye, and the description confirms it's what you want.

They work together, alongside the parameters. A clear name plus a clear description makes the right choice obvious.

On Databricks, when `UCFunctionToolkit` turns a Unity Catalog function into a tool, the description comes from the function's comment. So the comments you write are really part of your prompt. Make them clear.

check:0:0.a:
Superset gets one thing right. It makes sure both expected tools were called. If the agent skipped the identity check entirely, superset would catch that and fail the test.

But superset ignores **order**. It only asks "did every expected tool show up somewhere?" So this path would pass:

```
expected: check_identity, refund
actual:   refund, check_identity
```

Both tools were called, so superset gives a ✓. Yet the refund happened *before* the identity check. That is exactly the mistake the rule exists to prevent.

Superset also allows extra calls. An agent that refunded twice, or called some unrelated tool along the way, would still pass. For a required procedure, you usually want to flag that too.

So superset suits tasks where an extra lookup is harmless and order doesn't matter. A refund rule is not that kind of task.

Strict is better because it requires the same tools in the same order, so a refund that comes before the identity check fails the test.

check:0:1.a:
"Unordered" gets part of the job right. It checks that the agent called the same tools as the reference path, each the same number of times. So it would catch an agent that skipped the identity check entirely. It would also catch one that refunded twice.

But it ignores order. That is the whole point of this rule. Picture these two paths:

```
expected: check_identity, refund
actual:   refund, check_identity
```

Same tools, once each, so "unordered" says ✓. Yet the agent sent the money before it knew who it was talking to. That is exactly the mistake the rule exists to prevent, and the test would let it through.

A test that passes a dangerous path is worse than no test, because it makes you feel safe. When the rule is "this must happen before that," the order is the thing you need to check.

"Strict" is better because it requires the same tools in the same order, so a refund before the identity check fails the test.

check:1:1.a:
`superset` points the check the wrong way for this task.

**What `superset` checks:** every expected tool was called. Extra calls are fine.

**Why that misses here:** the danger for a read-only agent is an *extra* tool, like one that writes or deletes data. `superset` lets extras through without a complaint. Say the expected list is `search_docs, read_file` and the agent calls `search_docs, read_file, delete_record`. `superset` gives that a ✓, even though the agent just did the one thing it must never do.

**It also gets the other half wrong:** the task says the agent may skip tools. `superset` fails any run that skips an expected tool. So if the agent only calls `search_docs`, `superset` gives a ✗, even though that run was perfectly safe.

So `superset` blocks the harmless case and allows the harmful one. The one thing it shares with the right answer is that it compares the run against the expected list. It just compares in the wrong direction.

**Why `subset` fits:** it passes only if every tool the agent actually called was on the allowed list, so skipping is fine but a stray tool fails.

check:1:2.a:
"Strict" gets one thing right. It would catch an agent that calls a tool not on its list. Any extra call makes the two lists different, so the run fails. The risky behavior would never slip through.

The problem is that it fails too much. Strict demands the same tools in the same order as the reference path, the example path you compare against. This task says the agent may skip some tools. Say the list is `search_docs`, `read_file`, `read_table`, and the agent only needs `read_file` to answer. That run is perfectly safe, but strict marks it as a failure. It would also fail a run that used the right tools in a different order.

So strict punishes harmless differences. You would get a lot of false alarms, which are failures that aren't real problems. Real issues get harder to spot among them.

"Subset" is the better fit. It checks exactly the rule you care about: every tool the agent called was on the allowed list, and skipping some is fine.

check:2:0.a:
"Strict" gets a lot right here. It demands the exact tools from the reference path. It allows no extra calls, and it makes sure each tool appears the right number of times. So it would catch an agent that skipped `lookup_customer` or called `lookup_order` twice.

The problem is the one thing strict adds on top: order. Strict also says the tools must come in the same order as the reference path. Say your reference is `lookup_order`, then `lookup_customer`. An agent that calls `lookup_customer` first and `lookup_order` second does everything the task asks. Strict would still mark it as a failure.

That's a "false alarm": the check fails when nothing is actually wrong. False alarms waste your time and make you trust the evaluator less.

Strict is the right pick when order really matters, like checking identity before a refund. This task says either one can go first, so order isn't part of what "correct" means here.

"Unordered" is better because it checks for the same tools, each the same number of times, with nothing extra, and it ignores the order the task said doesn't matter.

check:2:1.a:

The problem is the phrase "once each and nothing else." `superset` allows extra calls. So it would pass a path like this:

```

```

That path calls `lookup_order` twice and adds a `refund` the task never asked for. `superset` sees both expected tools were called and gives a ✓. Your rule says that path is wrong.
